Cover Story · Issue 14 · Signal Decay

SIGNAL DECAY:
WHEN INTERFACES
START TO ROT

Software was supposed to be eternal — frictionless, weightless, clean. Instead it ages like everything else. A field guide to digital entropy, and why a generation of designers is learning to love the rot.

Words Jonah Marchetti Art Priya Venkat 8 min read June 2026

There is a particular sound a hard drive makes right before it dies — a faint, rhythmic tick, like a clock that has started to doubt itself. The first time I heard it I was nineteen, and I lost four years of photographs. The second time, I recorded it. I still play it sometimes. It is, I have decided, one of the most honest sounds a machine can make: the sound of something admitting it is mortal.

We do not like to think of our interfaces as mortal. The dominant aesthetic of the last fifteen years — call it the Great Flattening — was a promise of permanence. Soft shadows dissolved into nothing. Skeuomorphic leather and brushed metal were sanded down to clean rectangles. Everything became weightless, frictionless, a sheet of glass with helpful text floating behind it. The screen stopped pretending to be an object and started pretending to be air.

The Myth of the Clean Slate

Clean was never neutral. Clean was a worldview. It said: this product has no history, no labor, no body. It arrived fully formed from the cloud, and it will live there forever, updating itself in the night like a benevolent ghost. There is no rot here. There is no decay. There is only the eternal present of the well-funded roadmap.

Marginalia: The phrase "the cloud" is itself a decay-resistant metaphor — vaporous, edgeless, impossible to picture aging. Compare it to "the server farm," which smells of dust and burning fans.

But interfaces do rot, and we all know it. We feel it in the app that hasn't been updated since 2019 and now renders its buttons half off the screen. We feel it in the cracked tablet propped behind every café counter, its screen a constellation of dead pixels, still loyally taking orders. We feel it in the screenshot folder thirty thousand images deep, an archaeological record of every UI that has ever briefly governed our attention.

Polish is a lie a product tells about its own future.

Entropy as a Medium

A small, stubborn movement of designers has decided to stop fighting this. If decay is inevitable, they reason, then decay is a material — and materials can be composed. They are building interfaces that wear, that accrue texture with use, that show their seams on purpose. Buttons with visible registration errors, as if Riso-printed. Type that frays at the edges. Loading states that hiss with deliberate static.

Three signs you are looking at intentional rot

First: the grain is doing work. Real digital entropy is ugly and random; designed entropy has rhythm. When the noise feels composed — when the grain moves with the content rather than against it — somebody chose it. Second: the imperfection is consistent. A single glitch is an accident; a system of glitches is a typeface. Third: it respects you. Good decay never sacrifices the thing you came to do. The button still works. The text is still legible, even when it pretends not to be.

Lagos, Pink Dust, One Risograph

I traveled to a studio in Lagos that has become a quiet pilgrimage site for this aesthetic — a third-floor room where four designers share a single, temperamental Risograph and a near-religious devotion to its imperfections. The machine misregisters constantly; the fluorescent pink ink ghosts across every page; it jams if you breathe wrong. "It has opinions," one of them told me, prying a crumpled sheet from its rollers with the patience of someone defusing a bomb. "We design with the opinions now. Not against them."

What struck me was how little of this was nostalgia. They were not trying to make 1970s ephemera. They were using an analog machine's stubbornness as a way to smuggle unpredictability back into a digital practice that had become too obedient. The Riso was a random-number generator with a personality. The decay was the point.

Marginalia: The studio's printer is named "Auntie." Auntie has, by their count, ruined exactly one important client deadline and saved at least four boring ones.

The Loud Interface Returns

Back home, I started noticing the rot everywhere — and noticing that I liked it. The music app that renders its waveform as deliberate static. The portfolio site whose cursor leaves a magnetic trail. The zine — this one, in fact — that breaks its own grid on every page and dares you to keep reading anyway.

None of this is an accident, and none of it is purely decorative. Loudness is a stance. In a feed engineered to be smooth, frictionless, and instantly forgettable, friction is how you make a thing memorable. Decay is how you prove a thing is real. And static — that faint, ticking, mortal sound — turns out to be the most human noise a machine can make.

I still have that recording of my dying hard drive. Lately I've been thinking about pressing it to vinyl. Something permanent, for the sound of something falling apart.

Jonah Marchetti is a writer and recovering UX designer based in Glasgow. This is his third piece for STATIC//NOISE. Next: browse the back catalogue →
